# pyi-deps

Generate the `hiddenimports` list PyInstaller cannot see for itself, by parsing
the code instead of trusting a hand-written list.

```bash
python -m pyi_deps --root src/runtime --out build/_deps.py
```

```python
# build/_deps.py — generated, imported by the entry script
# Generated by pyi_deps -- do not edit.
# Imported by the entry script so PyInstaller's static analysis sees these.
import bs4  # noqa: F401
import requests  # noqa: F401
import tiktoken  # noqa: F401
```

## The problem it solves

PyInstaller freezes an app by walking `import` statements from the entry script.
Anything it cannot see statically has to be named by hand:

| Setup | What PyInstaller sees |
| --- | --- |
| `import x` in the entry script | yes |
| `import x` in a module the entry script imports | yes |
| `runpy.run_path("runtime/main.py")` | **nothing inside that file** |
| `importlib.import_module(name)` from a plugin table | **no** |

The third row is the common one for launchers: one small entry script, the real
code shipped as loose files next to it. The build works, then the installed app
dies with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'logging.handlers'` on a code
path nobody exercised during the smoke test.

The fix everyone reaches for is a manually maintained hidden-import list. It is
correct the day it is written and wrong the first time someone in the runtime
tree adds an import — with no test failing, because the failure only appears in
a frozen build.

This tool turns that list into a scan. The generated module is imported by the
entry script, so PyInstaller's normal analysis picks the imports up from there:

```python
# entry script
import _deps  # noqa: F401  (generated at build time)
```

## Usage

```bash
# in the build script, right before PyInstaller runs
python -m pyi_deps --root stage/runtime --out stage/_deps.py \
    --local app --local config \
    --exclude PIL
```

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--root` | directory to scan recursively (`.py` only, `__pycache__` skipped) |
| `--out` | where to write the generated module |
| `--local` | top-level name that is part of the app, so never emitted (repeatable) |
| `--exclude` | import prefix to leave out of the build, e.g. `PIL` (repeatable) |
| `--no-submodules` | skip `from package import module` resolution (cross-builds) |
| `--include-stdlib` | also list `os`, `json`, … (off by default: the generated file is for dependencies) |

## Every import is wrapped in `try/except`

The scan cannot tell a required import from one the code guards itself:

```python
try:
    import win32api          # optional on this platform
except ImportError:
    win32api = None
```

A bare `import win32api` in the generated module would turn that optional
dependency into a hard requirement — and because the entry script imports the
generated module, the app would die at startup on exactly the machines the guard
was written for. So each name gets its own `try` block:

```python
try:
    import win32api  # noqa: F401
except ImportError:
    pass  # optional dependency: PyInstaller still sees the import
```

PyInstaller's analysis is static, so an import inside a `try` is still found and
still bundled; only the runtime behaviour changes. One `try` per name, not one
around the block: otherwise the first missing package would skip all the rest.

As a library:

```python
from pyi_deps import scan, render

names = scan("stage/runtime", local_modules={"app"}, exclude_prefixes=("PIL",))
Path("stage/_deps.py").write_text(render(names), encoding="utf-8")
```

## The submodule detail

`from Crypto.Cipher import AES` imports **a module**, not an attribute. PyInstaller
bundles `Crypto.Cipher` and the binding then fails at runtime, because `AES` is a
separate extension. The scanner asks `importlib.util.find_spec` whether each
imported name resolves to a module and, if so, emits the full dotted path
(`Crypto.Cipher.AES`) as well.

That check needs the packages installed on the scanning machine, which is why
`--no-submodules` exists for cross-builds. Note what it does: `find_spec("a.b.c")`
**imports `a.b`** to look inside it, so a package with import-time side effects
(reads config, opens a connection) runs them during the scan. Do the scan in the
same throwaway environment you build in, or pass `--no-submodules` and accept
losing the submodule hint.

## Limits

- Only static `import` / `from ... import` statements. `importlib.import_module(var)`
  with a runtime-computed name is still your problem.
- It collects *names*, not versions. Pair it with a pinned requirements file.
- A syntax error in the tree is surfaced, not skipped: a broken file at build
  time is better than a missing import at run time.
